language_wrapper:
In base-{base}, consider all reduced proper fractions m/n with 1 ≤ m < n and gcd(m,n)=1. Write the base-{base} expansion of m/n as 0.d1 d2 d3 …, where the expansion has a non-repeating prefix of length ℓ (depending only on n and {base}) followed by a repeating cycle. Fix the digit pattern {pattern} (digits interpreted in base {base}). Find the smallest positive integer n for which there exists some m with gcd(m,n)=1 and m<n such that both of the following hold:
- the pattern {pattern} occurs consecutively as a block of digits that crosses the boundary between the non-repeating and repeating parts (i.e., some of its digits lie at positions ≤ ℓ and some at positions > ℓ), and the starting index of that occurrence is congruent to {residue1} modulo {modulus1};
- the pattern {pattern} also occurs entirely within the repeating part (at a position ≥ ℓ+1), and the starting index of that occurrence is congruent to {residue2} modulo {modulus2}.
Indices are counted starting from 1 for the first digit after the radix point. Answer with the minimal such n.
hardness_rationale: The seed problem asks for the smallest denominator n such that some reduced fraction m/n has a decimal expansion containing a specific three-digit block anywhere. Our augmentation simultaneously: (1) generalizes to arbitrary base 9 or 10; (2) requires a longer pattern (length 4 or 5); (3) imposes two separate positional constraints—one occurrence must straddle the preperiod-to-period boundary and another must lie wholly within the periodic part; and (4) constrains both starting indices by modular arithmetic conditions. Solving such an instance demands understanding the decomposition of denominators into parts dividing powers of the base versus coprime parts, the length of the non-repeating prefix, and the periodic remainder cycle. It also involves carefully tracking remainders to quantify the repetend and verifying congruence conditions on indices. These layers make the problem significantly more complex than the seed and preclude trivial guessing, aligning with advanced contest difficulty.
notes: Proof sketch and correctness: For a fixed base b and n, write n = A·B where all prime factors of A divide b and gcd(B, b) = 1. The base-b expansion of any m/n (with gcd(m, n) = 1) has a non-repeating prefix of length ℓ equal to the minimal t with A | b^t. This follows from clearing factors dividing b by multiplying m/n by successive powers of b; once the denominator’s b-power components are absorbed, the remainder dynamics depend solely on B. After ℓ digits, the remainders follow r_{k+1} ≡ b r_k (mod n) and the residual dynamics modulo B induce a cycle whose length is the multiplicative order of b modulo B; thus, the expansion becomes purely periodic beyond ℓ. Our verifier computes ℓ via prime exponents and detects the period by cycling remainders starting from the remainder after ℓ digits (r_ℓ). The straddle condition is satisfied exactly when there exists a start s with s ≤ ℓ < s+L−1 matching the pattern, and the congruence s ≡ residue1 (mod modulus1). The repeating-part condition is satisfied by scanning indices s ≥ ℓ+1 (over one or two periods) and requiring both the pattern match and s ≡ residue2 (mod modulus2). Minimality of n is enforced by searching n in increasing order and checking all coprime numerators m; the first n that admits such an m is returned. Because ℓ depends only on n and b and the repeating part behavior is captured by the remainder-cycle method, the algorithm is correct. The instance difficulty is further ensured by requiring ℓ ≥ 1 (straddling impossible otherwise) and a non-zero period (terminating expansions are rejected). Implementation notes: Trial division suffices for factoring in the bounded search. Digits are generated via standard long division in base b: from remainder r, set r ← b r, emit d = ⌊r/n⌋, update r ← r mod n. The cycle length is detected by recording remainders until the starting remainder repeats. The generator retries randomly and uses curated fallbacks to maintain high success rates while keeping instances non-trivial.
source_question: The decimal representation of $m/n,$ where $m$ and $n$ are relatively prime positive integers and $m < n,$ contains the digits 2, 5, and 1 consecutively, and in that order. Find the smallest value of $n$ for which this is possible.
